title: Inside the Exclusive Nathan Fielder Interview
gist: In this episode of WIRED's Uncanny Valley podcast, Katie Drummond describes her secret, NDA-bound interview with Nathan Fielder about his Elizabeth Holmes documentary and WIRED's reckoning with its early hype of Theranos. The hosts are skeptical of recent tech-billionaire giveaways: Anthropic's 5% share pledge to a public benefit fund, Elon Musk's promise of a SpaceX share for every US child, and a reported OpenAI idea of a 5% government stake. They read these as image management ahead of an IPO and midterms where AI and data centers are unpopular. They also cover a WIRED investigation into suspicious white-powder letters sent to election offices in at least 32 states.

insights.claim: Anthropic announced it will commit 5% of its company shares to a public benefit fund meant to address AI's impact on the labor market. According to Anthropic's statement, the fund could make charitable donations or direct money to "specific populations," but implementation details are sparse.
insights.speaker: Brian Barrett
insights.so_what: AI labs are starting to pre-empt the political backlash over labor displacement with equity-funded redistribution schemes.
insights.quote: Anthropic said it would commit 5 percent of its shares to a public benefit fund meant to address AI's impact on the labor market
insights.locator: Shifting gears to current tech companies

insights.claim: Elon Musk posted on X that next year he will give one SpaceX share to every child in America. Brian Barrett estimates that is about $10 billion at the current stock price, or 0.5% of SpaceX stock, but only about $150 per recipient.
insights.speaker: Brian Barrett
insights.so_what: The pledge implies a SpaceX valuation of about $2 trillion, but the hosts doubt it will happen.
insights.quote: It's $10 billion or so based on the current stock price. But it's 0.5 percent of overall SpaceX stock
insights.locator: And even if he does, it is a lot of money

insights.claim: Leah Feiger dismisses Elon Musk's SpaceX-share pledge as not credible, calling it "clearly not occurring" and saying Musk is famously anti-philanthropy.
insights.speaker: Leah Feiger
insights.so_what: Musk's promises should be discounted when assessing SpaceX dilution or retail-ownership effects.
insights.locator: Oh my god, yeah. That doesn't even count to me.

insights.claim: Brian Barrett argues that Anthropic's share pledge amounts to a private universal basic income controlled by Anthropic. In his view, it assumes AI will eliminate jobs and puts astonishing power in the company to decide both how AI reshapes society and who gets taken care of.
insights.speaker: Brian Barrett
insights.so_what: Expect political and regulatory scrutiny of AI labs that set themselves up as social-safety-net providers.
insights.quote: But it's UBI as dictated by Anthropic.
insights.locator: Yeah. And even if it did, it would be 150 bucks

insights.claim: Citing Matt Levine in Bloomberg's Money Stuff, Brian Barrett says each giveaway reflects its sponsor's self-image. Anthropic's says only it is responsible enough, Musk's reflects individual entrepreneurship, and OpenAI's reported July idea of a 5% US government stake (per the Financial Times) signals cooperation with government.
insights.speaker: Brian Barrett
insights.so_what: This is a lens for reading how each AI player positions itself toward the state as regulation takes shape.
insights.locator: One thing that's kind of fun here

insights.claim: Brian Barrett argues that all the AI-company giveaway models presume a world where AI eliminates other sources of income.
insights.speaker: Brian Barrett
insights.so_what: AI leaders implicitly expect large-scale labor displacement, which is a macro scenario to monitor.
insights.quote: none of them probably great, because they all presume this world in which other sources of money are not going to be here because of AI
insights.locator: One thing that's kind of fun here

insights.claim: Leah Feiger questions whether OpenAI would still offer a 5% stake to a Democratic-controlled Congress. She notes that Trump is a lame-duck president whatever the midterm results, so AI firms' political appeals will have to change.
insights.speaker: Leah Feiger
insights.so_what: A shift in Congress after the midterms could change how AI firms deal with government and where policy goes.
insights.quote: Are you still promising that 5 percent if you're OpenAI to a Democratic-controlled Congress?
insights.locator: No, I think that's honestly a really smart way

insights.claim: Brian Barrett notes that many people at Anthropic are adjacent to effective altruism, whose priorities differ from conventional philanthropy. He says some deprioritize climate because they believe AI will solve it, so public-benefit money is likely to be steered away from problems assumed to be solvable by AI.
insights.speaker: Brian Barrett
insights.so_what: Climate philanthropy from tech is drying up as AI-optimist beliefs change how capital is allocated.
insights.locator: Yeah. And I think to your point about the climate thing

insights.claim: Leah Feiger says Anthropic is preparing for a trillion-dollar IPO. She frames its giveaway as timed image management while AI and data centers are unpopular across party lines ahead of the midterms.
insights.speaker: Leah Feiger
insights.so_what: Anthropic's IPO narrative faces reputational and political headwinds from AI's unpopularity.
insights.quote: Anthropic is preparing for a trillion-dollar IPO right now.
insights.locator: We live in an unregulated hellhole.

insights.claim: According to Leah Feiger, data centers and AI dominate concerns in at least some midterm polling, and AI use has become a bipartisan issue. She says big AI companies have made many people hate them remarkably quickly.
insights.speaker: Leah Feiger
insights.so_what: Bipartisan anti-AI sentiment raises regulatory and permitting risk for data center buildouts.
insights.quote: The use of AI is a bipartisan issue at this point, which is fascinating.
insights.locator: We live in an unregulated hellhole.

insights.claim: Leah Feiger argues that tech philanthropy has stalled compared with a decade ago, when the Gates Foundation and climate giving were prominent. She says tech companies are also shutting down internal CSR complaint channels, so the new pledges look like headline grabs from firms that know they are unpopular.
insights.speaker: Leah Feiger
insights.so_what: Treat tech pledges as reputational defense rather than lasting commitments of capital.
insights.quote: It's the idea that like, oh, OK, we're actually that unpopular that we need to weigh in to some respect.

insights.claim: A WIRED investigation by David Gilbert, which contacted officials in all 50 states and DC, found that election offices in at least 32 states received suspicious letters, some containing white powder, two weeks before the midterms. The count could rise.
insights.speaker: Leah Feiger
insights.so_what: Disruption to election administration raises the risk of contested results and post-election volatility.
insights.locator: Last week, an official in the Louisiana Secretary of State's Office

insights.claim: The white-powder letters were matched by similar letters to congressional offices of both parties. The Postal Service intercepted most of them, but some election offices still had to evacuate, and the FBI has not said whether it has leads.
insights.speaker: Leah Feiger
insights.so_what: Election administrators are overstretched, and threats are adding to pressure on operations.

insights.claim: A letter intercepted in Utah, posted by Lt. Gov. Deidre Henderson, bore a Democratic Socialists of America return address, and DSA denied involvement. Leah Feiger calls it a literal false flag meant to deepen national divisions, similar to past foreign disinformation campaigns.
insights.speaker: Leah Feiger
insights.so_what: False-flag tactics increase polarization and the risk of disputed elections.
insights.quote: this is a literal false flag

insights.claim: Leah Feiger reports that NGOs, local activists and election officials find get-out-the-vote efforts hard amid threats and rumors of ICE at the polls. DHS officials say they don't plan to send immigration officers en masse to patrol polls.
insights.speaker: Leah Feiger
insights.so_what: Intimidation could reduce turnout, adding uncertainty to midterm outcomes.
insights.locator: Oh my God, I mean, that's the fear.

themes.theme: WIRED's Theranos reckoning and the Fielder film

insights.claim: Nathan Fielder and Lance Oppenheim's documentary You Can See Everything follows Fielder spending a month inside Elizabeth Holmes' home before she went to prison. It was kept secret for three years and seen by only a few dozen people before its Telluride debut, and WIRED had to sign an NDA before even learning it was a film.
insights.speaker: Brian Barrett
insights.so_what: Interest in founder-fraud stories remains high, and Theranos is still the reference case.
insights.locator: If you've been online this past week

insights.claim: Katie Drummond says WIRED in the early 2010s worked in a culture that lionized startup founders without enough scrutiny, and that Elizabeth Holmes played into it effectively. Today's WIRED would set a much higher bar before covering a precommercial startup like Theranos.
insights.speaker: Katie Drummond
insights.so_what: Tech media has turned more skeptical of founders, so expect tougher coverage of hyped startups.
insights.quote: there's a lot more necessary skepticism of these people and their ideas and where this money is coming from
insights.locator: Yeah. When I read Adam's story

insights.claim: Katie Drummond notes that after her joking Fielder interview, her Google search results now lean toward "Katie Drummond felon". Brian Barrett jokes that AI overviews will brand her a felon forever.
insights.speaker: Katie Drummond
insights.so_what: This illustrates the reputational risk when AI search summaries misread tone.
insights.locator: If I could clear up one thing

insights.claim: The PHP Foundation revealed two serious vulnerabilities that could affect millions of websites, part of what Leah Feiger describes as a recent wave of alarming hacking and vulnerability stories.
insights.speaker: Leah Feiger
insights.so_what: Widespread web-stack vulnerabilities support demand for security vendors and patching services.
insights.locator: So cute. So cute. There's candy everywhere.
